utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Witness, would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your witness, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But before I start, I would introduce to my left Ms. Diane Dicklich, who will take over the case manager function from Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have in front of you a piece of paper and on this piece of paper you have there the number 54, and that is the number you are referred to in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think everybody else in the courtroom has this sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, the name under this number, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the date under this name, is it your birth date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And there are also two other names under your birth date, and if you, in these proceedings, like to refer to these people, just do not tell us the name but the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to enter this sheet of paper as a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P398 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I was born in a village near Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I do, two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which neighbourhood did you live in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The neighbourhood of Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, the majority population was Muslim, but it was not ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Worker. Actually, I am a skilled worker by profession, but I was in charge of a shift in a factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the war start in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, as far as the date of the beginning of the war in Foca is concerned, we could talk about that a lot. However, I experienced my first shelling on the morning of the 6th of April, around 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where were you when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In the apartment. In my apartment where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it an apartment block or was it a small building you lived in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: An apartment block with some 29 apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the people living in this apartment block, were they ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you do when the fighting started? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The basement, with all the other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The people in the basement, what ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, they belonged to different ethnic groups, but there were far more Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many Serbs were among the people in the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Three or four persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why so few?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know why so few. I really don't know the right answer to that. However, I imagine that knowing what would happen, they went away during the weekend. They went to stay with some relatives. They sent their families away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean actually there were more people living in the -- more Serb people living in the apartment block but they were gone when the war started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, yes. A lot of attention was paid to that before, that buildings should not be ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I mean the former Yugoslavia was well known for tensions that existed in the Second World War. Later on, the government paid attention that all ethnic groups be represented at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Which part of the town was shelled? Was it all over the town the shelling or in particular parts? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know that all of Donje Polje was shelled. I cannot say what happened up there in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were houses destroyed during the initial fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Serb houses among those destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I didn't see any. There weren't any private Serb homes in that neighbourhood. Perhaps about ten in that part of the neighbourhood that I lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the house of the accused Krnojelac was destroyed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know. I know something that will be seen later. I know that some camp inmates went to repair the house of the mentioned person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did the fighting last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, seven or eight days. I don't know exactly. I think it was from the 6th until the 14th or 15th of April, something like that, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Muslims withdraw from Foca or flee from Foca at a point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: A lot of people did. During the night, they went to Gorazde. Some remained, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After the Muslims had fled, did this take an end to the shelling or did it, nevertheless, continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. No. That was not an end to the shelling. On the contrary. The shelling was with some kind of inflammable shells. The shooting went on. So whatever was not destroyed at first was totally destroyed and burned down then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that, this particular kind of shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: 14th, 15th, 16th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the houses in Donje Polje neighbourhood in general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: January?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was obviously a mistake in the interpretation. In general, I said, to the whole of the Muslim houses of Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, what was not destroyed by the shelling was burned down later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know that because I saw it. I could see it from my terrace. I'm talking about the part of the neighbourhood that I lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the other Muslim neighbourhoods? Did you see what happened to these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. I didn't even move about there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened to the mosques? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know only about two mosques for sure. I saw that they were no longer there. One is near the former kindergarten and the other one is near the former bus station. I don't know whether it's still a bus station.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you see these mosques being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did not see these mosques being destroyed; I was in the KP Dom camp. However, when we travelled by bus, on the 30th of August, 1992, I saw this. These two mosques no longer existed; it was just empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that many Muslims fled to Gorazde but you were among those who stayed. Did you stay in Donje Polje or did you go somewhere else within Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I stayed in Donje Polje for one night after that together with my neighbour - I don't know whether I should mention his name or not; he's a Serb - and then I went to a different part of the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Cohodar Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is this a Muslim neighbourhood or a mixed neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: A mixed neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: My daughter lived there. We talked on the phone, and she told me the situation was much better there and that I would be much safer there. (redacted) and went to live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were in KP Dom. When were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: On the 16th of August -- oh, what am I saying? Sorry. On the 16th of April, in Cohodar Mahala, that neighbourhood that I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What time of the day were you arrested; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I think it was just before noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you were arrested in this Cohodar Mahala neighbourhood. In your daughter's home or where? Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was taken out of the house, myself, her husband, and his uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Persons unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they policemen or soldiers or civilian persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They had some kind of olive-green/grey uniform that belonged to the JNA, that I used to wear before. They were in camouflage uniforms. Nobody wore civilian clothes or a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you did not know them. Does that mean they were not from Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Those who arrested us were not from Foca for sure. However, I'm not claiming that I have to know all the people from the territory of the municipality of Foca, which is very big from a human and geographical point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the soldiers tell you why you were arrested and what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, my wife and daughter started to wail and they asked what would happen to us, and then they said they would return us after we make statements. And about 150 metres away, in the yard, there were already people gathered there and there were more and more people coming, and I saw, recognised, two men I knew. That was Ranko Pijano -- Ranko Pijano and Puko Mitrasinovic, Goran Mitrasinovic, called Puko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Goran Mitrasinovic was a worker, as far as I know. Perhaps he went to work elsewhere afterwards; he worked in Sipad Maglic before. Ranko Pijano was a lawyer in the former Focatrans, and then when the firm split up, then he was in the Viner firm and he worked in some of the services there. He was some kind of secretary or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you saw them, were they also in uniform? And if so, which uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, yes. SMB, olive-green/grey, military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever find out what the charges against you were and why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, no, I never found out. I was not accused and I did not stand trial, ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned other people being gathered already in a yard. How many people were gathered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: When I arrived, perhaps 50 people or even more; but finally, when they took us to the KP Dom, I think there were almost 200 people. Perhaps a bit more; perhaps a bit less. But you have to understand the situation as it was. Nobody counted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were only male people being gathered there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you know what ethnicity these people had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: All.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what ages did these people have, between the youngest and the oldest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, from the age of 16 or 17 up to 80. How could I know? My son-in-law's uncle was 75, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, no, I never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you take part in the fighting in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And of those people you knew among those gathered there in the yard, can you say if they were civilians, or were there fighters among you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Civilians. Civilians only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there anything particular about you and these other men that you had in common that might have been a reason for the arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, probably the reason was because they were Muslims. I don't know what other reason there could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this day when you were arrested, were you mistreated by the soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Not at that place, at least I did not notice over there at that place, as we were waiting for the buses to take us to the camp. However, in the camp, as we were entering the compound, we went in through the gate where the furniture was being taken out. Usually, we were beaten up a bit as we were getting out of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you were taken there in a bus or several buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: There were two buses; one belonged to the National Park of Sutjeska and the other one to the Focatrans work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the buses drive into the KP Dom compound, or did you leave the buses in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, they entered the compound of the KP Dom. I said a few minutes ago that this was at the gate which was a big gate, a sliding door as well, and I think that the furniture used to be taken out through there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were all beaten when you left the buses. Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In my opinion, those were persons from Serbia for the most part, because they spoke with the accent that people from there use. I didn't know anyone personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those who beat, were they all soldiers, or did you see any regular guards present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, no, at that time I did not see any guards, and I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken within the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness now Exhibit 18, photo 7512. This is the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the photo and please tell us if you can see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can you show us the Room number 11 on this photo? Is it in building number 1 or building number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The building marked number 1. But here, on this photograph, you can hardly see. It is mainly these windows there facing the garden, a bit further down here, yes. And then there are windows down here, facing administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the building with the number 1 on top of it and it's actually the building we refer to as A.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, for the rest of your testimony, please have in mind that for us it is building A. And the witness is pointing at the ground floor of this building. Witness, did you always stay in this Room 11 or were you transferred to another room at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I was in Room number 20 very briefly, for about three days, and then for three or four days in solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you show us the Room number 20 on this photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is also pointing to the second floor. To make it clear, the second floor also from the top, seen from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in Room number 20, could you see the Drina River and the bridge over the Drina in front of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think you can see it, although I did not look much at the time. I was given work assignments, and I was very tired, and I spent only three days there. I didn't look.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness now the photo 7476.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you look at this photo? You can see the arrows on the photo. What room are they pointing at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, you can. May I begin to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: These arrows are pointing for windows. The two to the right are -- belong to one dormitory and the other two to the other room -- dormitory in Room 11, and below that is the storage space.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The storage space, did you ever look into it? Was it full or was it empty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: While I was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. No. No. I had no access there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now I would like to show you another photo, and it's the photo 7483. It's the top photo. You can see a door, and it's a little bit hard to see, but on the original you can see that there is a number 11 on the door. Did the door --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I guess so, because all the rooms have such doors, identical doors. There is nothing to tell me whether this is a door to Room 11 or not. I think that on the opposite side, the door to Room 12 is the same. I can't see the number here. I cannot see the number. It doesn't help that you zoomed it in. I cannot see the number really. So it could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And yet I would like to show you a floor plan that was made by a witness before you, and I would like to show you the floor plan 6/2. Please have a look at the prisoners' building. Can you tell us where Room 11 is and if it is drawn in correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think these two rooms here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean? What are these two rooms there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Why, the two rooms here on this side are two dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Room 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, there has been no dispute that that is Room 11, and it's been shown to a number of witnesses. They're obviously two dormitories. I think one of the witnesses described them as bedrooms that belonged to Room 11. There's been no dispute at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, Your Honour, but I would want the witness to discuss in which room he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but you start off by looking at it from the outside, and then this. We'd get along a lot more quickly if you go straight to this and say, "This is Room 11," and, "Which room were you in?"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't have to worry about leading where there is something which is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said two bedrooms, but actually, weren't there even four bedrooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: On this side. Listen, on this side towards the administrative part of the camp and two on that side. I slept here, for instance. But all this was an area which the inhabitants of Room 11 could use. This was used for leisure activities by former convicts who had normal living conditions, if we can put it that way. But this is the entrance here. This is a small entry, and here the wash basin and the WC.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness. So you could move around in all four bedrooms --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. The witness had just explained which dormitory he was in, and we cannot read -- understand it through the transcript unless it is explained. He just pointed at the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're quite right, and you probably had a better view of it than we did because you would have heard it in the original B/C/S. He was moving the pointer at the time the translation came through, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. If you want to know which bedroom he's in, let's just ask that question and ask him to hold the pointer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in which bedroom did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Sleep. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the bedroom going to the back side, and it's the left bedroom going to the back side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In the corner of the building, I think, might be the best way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In the corner of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you also went into the other two bedrooms who faced the administration building? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The remaining three. Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let me now show you two photos, actually. One photo is the photo 7495 and the other one is the photo 7503.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness shown them next to each other. Only the bottom photos, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom photos, and in relation to the windows, could you say which bedroom is which from the position of the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: From the position of the windows, one cannot really conclude anything because they're identical in both rooms. This was -- these photographs were taken from within the rooms. If I were outside, perhaps I could identify them, but otherwise, they're identical. So I just don't know. You have windows here and you have windows there, even though I think that the one to the left -- that the one to the right was on the corner of the building. As a matter of fact, they all take the corner, either the left one or the right one. But such an inside look doesn't really help you identify because the windows are identical and all these beds, of course, can be positioned wherever at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. It may be if we had a look at the photograph on the right a little bit more carefully, there appears to be a window on the right wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's what I just wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, look at the photo 7495 first alone. Yes. Yes. Maybe this is better. Please have a look at the position of the windows. On the lower photo, do you see that there are windows on the right side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I see something here. This is the right-hand side if you look at it from inside the room. But if I looked at it from the administrative building, then this would be to the -- this would be on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, are we not having the photographer to tell us all of this? What is the necessity of getting it from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like the witness to point out where he was standing when a certain incident happened. I would like to, but okay, we can move on. I thought he would see it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: This room which you see on the lower photograph, that is not my room because it did not have any windows on the right. From this angle, it had windows overlooking the compound, the park, and these here overlook the administrative building. The two windows on the left, they have a view of the park.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on. I would like to show you now the window -- not the window, sorry, the photo 7499. That's the lower one. Does this view look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. This is the ground floor and the upper floor, right below one of the dormitories, perhaps not more than ten metres as the crow flies. And to the left, you cannot see it on this photograph, but there is a door into the compound somewhere here; you cannot see it on this photograph. From the camp compound, that is how you enter the administrative part of the building here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Would that be the view you had from one of the bedrooms in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, this part is what you can see from both those bedrooms. But I was -- again, if we look from the administrative part towards the dormitory, when this incident happened about which I guess you want to ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And another photo, I would like to show you another photo, and that's the photo 7479. Can you say which view it is? Did you have such a view from Room 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, yes, this I could see. This is from one of the bedrooms in Room 11, which we just saw a moment ago. This is a view of the compound, and these stairs lead from -- below here are the stairs. This is the park with a path, and this is how we went up into the room. This is a view of the restaurant and factories. That was the factory. This is the -- to the right is the canteen, and then the rest of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: A diagonal view.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And you just mentioned a door that you could see from Room 11, and I would like to show you a last photo, and that's the photo 7473. That is the lower photo. On this photo, the door close to number 1, is that the door you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when you arrived in Room 11, were there already detainees in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, some 30, 40 people, and many of us were brought there, so at that particular moment there were more than 100 men there. Much more than 100.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was the highest number of detainees that ever were in Room 11 at a time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think that it was the first day when they brought us in, and then they began the very next day to move people to other rooms. But I stayed in that room. Well, there were over 100. One-hundred and fifty men could have been there that first day and the next day because it was really very crowded. But in a day or two or three, I don't know, people were then put in other rooms, and after that it was always around 60, 70 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know why you stayed in Room 11? Could you see a system in moving the people to rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I wouldn't know why I stayed in Room 11. I wasn't the only one; there were many others who stayed there. I don't know the reason. I guess because it was just too crowded, that there was no where to lie down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The people in Room 11 who were there then for a longer time together with you, were they all Muslims, or were people of other ethnicity among you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In my room there was one Catholic, a Croat; Kruno Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the person in Schedule C, number 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In what health state was Mr. Marinovic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In a very poor state; beaten over, his cheekbone broken, many bruises on his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The other people in the room, what age did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They belonged to all age groups. The eldest ones were 70, 75 and the youngest, around 16, I think. There was a boy, Soro, who was 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What state of health did these other people have? Were there sick people among you, handicapped people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: At that time there were no sick people there, I mean people who would have to lie down because of a fever or something. But afterwards people gradually lost strength, lost weight, and quite a number of them were beaten many times over.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Marinovic. How old was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, he could have been a year or two, maybe four or five younger than I am, but that is only my opinion. He could have been four or five years my junior, perhaps more -- no, not more. But he's younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was he? What was his profession; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think -- I know what he did of late. He was a mechanic; he repaired TV receivers and things like that. Before that he worked for Zenica TV, for Sarajevo TV, and he was a lighting master. I think that's what you call it but I'm not sure. I do not know whether this is the term, really, but he was responsible for lighting, when you work with lights, when you want to shoot something. He was also a journalist a little bit. He dabbled in journalism. As a matter of fact, I do not really know him. But one man, I think, threatened him, "Uh-huh, you've written," and it was published in Zagreb or something. But whether he was a professional journalist or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he was injured. Did he get medical care for his injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see how many detainees were in the other rooms? Could you estimate altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: At that moment, no. At that moment, no, because people were being brought in or out all the time. But later, after perhaps 15, 20 days, perhaps a month, because of the position of Room 11, we tried to count people. Once we counted 700, 708, 705, but it does not mean that it was really very accurate. There could have been more men or a less, perhaps a few more or a few less.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As far as you knew those people you saw, did they all come from Foca and the surrounding villages, or did they also come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were people from Foca and adjacent villages. But of course it is quite possible that they were -- oh, yes, yes, yes -- sorry, yes. A busful of people came with people from the Montenegrin coast, people who were from Gorazde, Cajnice, Srebrenica, Trebinje. As far as I can remember, those men had fled there and registered with the Red Cross, but somehow people went there and rounded up some 50 of them. And I know that there was one from Trebinje, four or five from Srebrenica, four or five, as far as I know, from Gorazde, and two, three from Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did these people arrive? When did these detainees arrive in KP Dom? Do you remember the month, maybe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Perhaps late May or early June. I wouldn't know; I really wasn't up to any statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were women ever detained in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: All I know is that one night a busload of women and children was brought there in late evening and so they spent the night in the compound, but they were not there after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that in the beginning there were these soldiers there. While these soldiers were there, did any beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It was a daily occurrence, in passing, yes, but they did not stay long. I mean, I don't claim it was a day or two more, a day or two less, or ten days, but they took over the -- but then the camp was taken over by policemen, that is, former policemen. There were not many. There were also some other people who were milling about, but they were, by and large -- the guards were, by and large, the former guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did they take over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, say, for about ten days, seven, eight, ten days -- seven, eight days after the camp was established, and I think it began to be settled then. They were Serbs, and they used the dialect that is not spoken in Foca so I assumed that they came from Serbia, because that is where they use this dialect. Moreover, some of them talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you here. I was asking you about the guards who took over, and you said that they were the former guards you knew. What kind of uniforms did they wear, the former prison guard uniforms or military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniforms, except one or two who were in camouflage uniforms. But otherwise they were guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they police uniforms or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they have, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Do we begin with the knives or pistols or Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just tell us what you saw on the guards as weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, say, they had, if you call it a weapon, the axe handles, for instance, and knives. Often they would throw knives at the acacias. And they had pistols and automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there any Serb prisoners in the KP Dom while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Some men were singled out there. They did not mix with us. There were some people, and I knew two or three of them. One even cried to me as I was coming from the canteen. He said, "Hey," and mentioned my name, and said, "Look, I'm here too. They locked me because I wouldn't take up the rifle."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where were these Serb prisoners kept, in which part of KP Dom? Do you know the room number or the wing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know which room -- which number of the room. I know they were in the wing where these solitary confinement cells were, only above it, on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The solitary confinement cells, in which building were they, in the building A where Room 11 was or in the other wing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Neither in building A with Room 11 nor B with Room 20. There is a separate wing which is the transfers wing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Have you ever been take taken to these isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the floor plan 6/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please have a look at this floor plan. And can you show us --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have to move it a little bit. You have to move it to the left. Yes. No, the other way. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you show us -- do you recall in which isolation cell you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think the last one here, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes. Thank you. And now I would like to show you two photos, and it is 7525 and 7526. Please have a look at the photos and tell us if the isolation cell you were in looked kind of similar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: This is solitary confinement, a solitary confinement cell, its inside. I think it is self-explanatory. You see how dirty the toilet is. You can't see it on this photograph here, but there should be a faucet here that can be opened, but you can't really see anything here. There is something black here and then this is the toilet. This is what it looked like in my cell at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Why? Well, I was supposed to work in the kitchen, and I worked on the distribution of food for three days. I felt sorry for person 115. I gave this person an extra slice of bread which was very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what happened? Did someone see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He saw it in his hands, and then he asked him, "Where did you get this?" Then he said he got it from the man who was distributing bread that day. That was Pilica Blagojevic. Pilica was his nickname. I can't remember his name any more. He was a guard. He came in there where the food was being distributed, and he asked who was handing out the bread, and I said, "I am." I didn't even know why he asked me. He told me to take off that white shirt and those white trousers and to report to Maric. And I asked where, and he showed me the direction in which this was. That is where the solitary confinement cells were. I did not know what this was all about. I reported to Maric, and he said, "What have you done?" And I said, "Nothing." "What have you done?" "Nothing." In the meantime, Pilica arrived and said that I gave bread to this person. Maric put me in there, locked me up. Pilica hit me a few times, hit me really bad. There were bruises and a few teeth out, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maric, who was that? Was that another guard in charge maybe of the cells or what? Who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was in charge of the cells. I think it was Milomir Maric, nicknamed Mara. I don't know whether he was in charge of the cells, but at that moment when I was taken to the cell, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So he was a guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He was a guard from before. He was a guard from before at the KP Dom, and he was there while I was at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did this happen, this incident in the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think on the 8th of August. I think. I think I started working at the kitchen on the 5th. I worked three days. It should have been then the 8th of August, 1992, of course. Everything that I'm talking about is the period between the 16th, 17th of April and the 30th of August, 1992. So let us avoid any kind of confusion. If I don't mention the year, all of it has to do with 1992. That is the period that I spent in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who gave you the kitchen job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Savo Todovic to me. But I don't know about the others. He was before also the officer for the division of labour in the KP Dom, and that is what he told us camp inmates to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ask him to get the job in the kitchen or did he just call you out and order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He sent one of the guards, I don't know which one, and he told me that I should come with him to Savo Todovic. I came there. That was also where Maric was when I was going there. There are these officers there who could remember all of it now. And I when arrived, he said to me that he was appointing me to distribute food, but, unfortunately, this lasted only for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While he appointed you doing this job, did he warn you? Did he give you a directive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. He warned me that I should not do what I did, that I could lose my head if I were to give someone more food or an extra slice of bread. Yes. Yes, but that really didn't remain imprinted in my memory, so what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were beaten and that you lost some teeth and you had bruises. Was it -- were you only beaten this one time or were you beaten several times while in the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I was only beaten then by Blagojevic, and nobody else ever beat me, because I did not stay in solitary confinement for long, three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And while you were in solitary confinement, were there other detainees as well in the adjacent cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: There were four or five cells there. They also say that also there were cells on the other side. Often beatings could be heard, but also conversations could be heard between cells, although people could not see each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see that anybody was beaten at the same time as you or in these few days or could you only hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I could only hear it. I could not see it because there are no windows there. There is just a very small opening on the door with glass and also mesh. But when I was there, I don't think there was even any glass. There was just this metal mesh.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who released you from the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic, commander of the guard, commander of the security. I don't know. Commander of these police who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he say anything to you when he released you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, he said, "You know what? I'm going to let you go although you were supposed to be killed, liquidated," something like that. I don't know. Something like that, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you more details about it, who told him that you were to be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we have already heard other witnesses speaking about the conditions in the KP Dom, and we do not have to repeat it. Did you lose weight while you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: To be precise, I lost 37 kilogrammes during my 136 days in the camp, at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Because of the poor food.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was no food available because of the war or were the rations deliberately kept so low? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this was intentional or unintentional, but food was scarce. It would be wrong for me to say that it was intentional now. I don't know that there was a scarcity of food. I don't know whether it was because of the war or because they wanted to starve people. I cannot say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any person died due to the conditions in the KP Dom? I'm not referring to violent acts. I'm referring to the conditions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Not in my room. However, it is well known that Eso Hodzic, as he was called -- he was a taxi driver before -- died because his ulcer perforated and he was not adequately taken care of. I don't know about other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you locked in the Room 11 all the time or were you taken out for walks in the yard while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. Only when we went to have meals, breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and sometimes when I went to unload flour. I went once. That's when I went out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have family visits at a point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Once. Once. I don't know exactly when this was. On the 9th of May, I think. I'm not sure of the date, but that was the first and last time my wife visited me. It was on the 9th of May, as far as I can remember. After that, visits were forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you request a visit or did your wife request permission to see you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, she probably did not request that. I didn't request that. However, this was an open visit in the part of the administrative building. It was very short, and a guard, a policeman, was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in the KP Dom, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that and where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, at the outset, I think, end of April, beginning of May perhaps. This was in the administrative part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Misa Koprivica, inspector of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "SUP," do you mean the police in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. The Secretariat of the Interior. That's the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did he want to know from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you he treated me quite fairly. His task was to ask me where I was, what I was doing, whether I was organised in some fashion. He even treated me to a cup of coffee and a cigarette, the man did. He treated me very fairly. However, I heard later from some others, now to what extent you can believe this or not is different, that he beat them. I did not see that, but he really did not treat me that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that others were beaten by him or claimed to have been beaten by him. Do you recall who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, the three Soro brothers were there and Cedic Elvedin, Dzemal Vahida. These are actually people who are from this neighbourhood of Cohodor Mahala. Now, whether he beat them, why he beat them, I don't know, but he did tell me as we were talking, "Imagine, at this old man's place we found a radio transmitter." And I said, "Oh, that's impossible. He doesn't even know how to turn on a regular radio to listen to the news. How could he know how to operate that?" "Oh, yes, he does," said he. "They found it there. And also in somebody else's house, in the basement, they found 100 kilogrammes of explosive." I don't know whether that's true or not, but I suppose that this man whom he described to me does not even know how to turn on a radio to listen to the news.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "he" told you, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Misa Koprivica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me clarify. When did he tell you that, while he was questioning you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to which old man do you refer? Can you give us the name of this old man who was supposed to have a radio transmitter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I can't say. It was the name of a man who I knew a very little bit. I don't know who it was, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see detainees being beaten in the prisoners' quarters, in the rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In the rooms, no. In Room 11, nobody was beaten in the room, but in the administrative building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was taken out of your room and taken to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Dzemal Vahida; Elvedin Cedic, Ekinda; Hadzic; Sahinovic were taken out on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us, Dzemal Vahida - that's number C-27 - when he was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Dzemal Vahida, when he was taken out for beatings, I can't remember the date, but it was in May for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that these people were taken out several times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see them return? Let's speak about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They returned. He, Dzemal Vahida, and Ekinda Cedic were returned, one after the other. One would be taken out and then the other one would be taken out when this one would be brought back, and that's the way it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ekinda Cedic, does he have a different name as well? Ekinda sounds to me like a nickname.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Ekinda is a nickname. Elvedin Cedic is his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the person C-5. Could you see what injuries they had when they returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Disastrous. Cedic had bruises on his head. He's a young man but he's kind of bald, and you could see it on his head and all over his body. Vahida also had bruises. And also up here, I mean his teeth had completely gone through his skin and his teeth were all broken, and he had to use a straw for drinking tea and soup for several days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they tell you where exactly they had been beaten, and who did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In one of the offices of the administrative part of the KP Dom. I don't know whether I'm going to remember the name anymore. Radivoje Elez, son of Gavro, nicknamed Mento. I don't know the others, but Mento was there for sure, because he said that Mento sort of swirled and kicked him when his teeth were broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you are talking about whom, Ekinda Cedic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, Dzemal Vahida, when his teeth were broken and when his remaining teeth were protruding from the skin of his upper lip.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Mento, was that a guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was it, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He was a young man. I don't know exactly. I think he worked as a carpenter before the war. But he came to administer justice, I guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said this happened in May. Was it during the daytime or during the night-time? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: During the day. During the day. During the day they would be taken out several times. One would be taken out and then he would be brought back in, and then the other one would be taken out and then brought back, and then the other one again. So alternately during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took them out of the rooms to the administration building? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know personally who did, but in most cases it was Slobodan Pejic/Boban Pejic, who took people out. He had a piece of paper with people's names on it. I think that in 90 per cent of all cases, as far as Room 11 is concerned, Boban Pejic/Slobodan Pejic took people from Room 11. I think that he was the youngest guard there and that is probably why he was assigned this duty to go up and down, up and down, up and down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any other detainee being taken in this manner and returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: People were taken many times. I saw Aziz Sahinovic, for example, and then this young Uzunovic. I can't remember his name right now; perhaps I'll think of it later. He is a medical worker. He was beaten up but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is the person C-26, and the witness is actually referring to incident 5.29 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Uzunovic come back, and did you see what injuries he had, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, primarily, these were bruises all over the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Azinovic, you mentioned. What kind of injuries did you see on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did not mention Mr. Azinovic. I think that this is a slip of the tongue. I mentioned Mr. Sahinovic. This is Aziz Sahinovic. Perhaps this was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was my wrong pronunciation, I'm sorry. So what did you see on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He was beaten up very badly; he was black and blue. But he complained about the area where the kidneys are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you who beat him up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. He said it was the guard Burilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you where it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In the administrative building, on the ground floor, somewhere where I had never been; where there were some kind of chains, where before they would tie up the detainees if they came in drunk, and they let them lie there on the concrete floor, chained, until they would get sober.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else return from the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Maybe I can't remember, but there were such cases, there really were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Let us now speak about those -- let us speak about another incident. Did you ever hear shots in the KP Dom in relation to beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know what you're getting at. There were lots of shots, shooting sort of into the air, in the evening when the guards would sit in front of the restaurant. But I know what you're getting at. I heard these shots. But there were shots, actually, when killings were committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like -- yes, that is actually what I'm referring to. Can you tell us if you ever saw people being shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, on the 25th of June I saw this. From 9.30 until 10.30, I think it was more like 10.00, from my room they took four -- three -- four men, and one was brought in from somewhere else. I knew all of them. They were taken to the administrative part of the building where you can see the broken glass on the window, the one I showed you a few minutes ago. In that area, they were first beaten up; they were choked, kicked, hit with hands and feet. And then they were made to stand against the wall with their hands up and they were shot with firearms. I have to mention that it rained very hard outside then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I go into the details of this incident, I see it's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is by my watch, if not by the clock. Yes, we'll take our adjournment now and resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, speaking about this incident on the 25th of June, 1992, who was taken out from your room? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They took Munib Veiz, Mustafa Kuloglija, Professor and engineer Kemal Dzelilovic, and the little Uzunovic. I can't remember his first name, but he was a nurse. Enes, Enes Uzunovic. Sorry, I just remembered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Munib Veiz, what was he by profession? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He was a salesman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Dzelilovic. You said professor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was an engineer and professor of mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mustafa Kuloglija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Kuloglija is a teacher by profession, and I believe he was responsible for elementary education in the municipal administration in Foca. And the little Uzunovic was a nurse, and he worked in the hospital. And another man, Hamid Ramovic, was taken together with them, but he was not from our room. However, I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was he? What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I believe he was a miner, a manual worker.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who called them out? Who called them out from your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Again, Slobodan Pejic, Boban. I don't know who took Ramovic, but Slobodan Pejic, nicknamed Boban, called out the names of those four from my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They were taken to the administrative part of the building, the ground floor that we saw awhile ago on that photograph, with that window on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness again, and it's the photograph 7499, the lower one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you show us where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to the second window on the ground floor, counted from the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How could you see that? Did you see them in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I saw them in that room, but they entered from somewhere here. The door is over here. You can't see it on the photograph. And there's a passage. And from that passage it goes through the administrative part of the building, from the street to the prison compound, and they were here in this, and that is where they were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you actually see them, and how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I saw them and I saw them well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the light on in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see anything else in the room which was maybe strange to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In that room -- I do not know what the lady asking me questions means, but during the night when the lights are out, you can still see very well because there are some control lights, something that radiated lights, some control instrument or something, something that produced a red light but not very powerful. These are something like these control lamps when you switch off your TV set, for instance, and then you see the red light. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see who beat them in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm afraid I won't be able to give you the names because it was eight and a half years ago. There was Dragomir Obrenovic, nicknamed Obren, guard; Burilo, guard; Zoran Matovic, guard; Rade Vukovic, guard; there was Predrag Stefanovic, Predo; and I can't remember others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you clearly see them, these guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed, very clearly. Well, that was their night-shift. That day they were on duty, and I could see them very well against the light. I watched it through the window of Room 11 on the left. It's perhaps less than 8 -- not as many as 8 or 10 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were these guards you mentioned and these detainees you mentioned, were they in this room all at the same time or were the detainees beaten one after another, separately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: All together they beat them. They were all together there. First they maltreated them and that was followed by what I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did they beat them, with objects for with their fists only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Fists and feet. Fists and feet. They would grab them by the throat, and then when firing started, I saw Zoran Matovic move his head, turn over his head with his foot to see whether he was alive still, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Whose head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Kemal Dzelilovic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did the beating last? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Some 10 minutes. It was all over in 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And could you hear the voices of the detainees or the guards? Could you hear what was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Nobody said anything. At least one could not hear anything. Some sounds, yes, but nothing that one could identify. Perhaps a wail, a sob, but that is not speech, just a cry of pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said they were shot. Did one guard shoot them or did several guards shoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: One could hear several shots simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the detainees fall down after the shots were heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did see that. There were no more people leaning against the wall; they were all on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see -- when this happened, could you see the entire bodies of the detainees and the guards or parts of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: When they were lying down on the floor, when they were dead, I suppose, one could see the heads of those which were farther away from us, and that is how I could see Zoka Matovic push his -- push Dzelilovic's head with his foot to see if he was alive. That is what I could see. I don't know. And then Zoka left, because there are stairs leading upstairs, and he carried several -- he had several blankets over his arm, something like army blankets, down the stairs. And one could see it all very well, how they put them there and then carried them out somewhere, and then one could hear a vehicle come and then disappear shortly afterwards. So it's the position that they just took them away somewhere. And after awhile, perhaps 10 or 15 minutes later, men came with buckets and mops or something, in olive-green/grey uniforms, and cleaned that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have shown us the window, and I would like you -- the window you looked through when this happened. I would like to show you again the floor plan, and this time it's Exhibit 6/1. I would like to ask you to look at the floor plan of the administration building. Are you able to point out the room? If not, it's ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I can't see much here, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe you can look actually on this drawing itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, this should be it. I kept looking here, but that's the canteen here, the restaurant. But it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just put it on the ELMO again. Could you see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, I can't see it once more. Now again I can't see it. Believe me, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe when you look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: This should be it. This should be it. Yes, now it's slightly larger.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you pointing at the second room from the left or to the third, where there is this little "TEL"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: From that photograph, through the window on that photograph you can see where this is very well. But here I just don't see any proper rooms. Well, you know, I'm really not accustomed to reading ground floor maps. On that photograph I can show you very well; however, on this plan, I really can't find my way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have a photograph of the administrative building from the detainees' point of view which shows more than just what we see looking out that window, which is the photograph we've been operating on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may assist the witness to identify the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have here the photo. That is the photo 7474 and 7475, and this may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, if you look first on the upper photo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For example, which is the window which appeared to have the broken glass?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is the third window from the left-hand side on the ground floor which is next to this water drain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: To the right of the water pipe?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, to the right of the water pipe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: That is the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's have a short look at the bottom photo. You see it's a little bit bigger. Is this the window left of the water pipe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Left of the water pipe, I think that's the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It is opposite, it is directly opposite the window through which I watched.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Usher. You can put all the photos away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that this was on the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you remember the date? Is there a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, there is a very good reason: because Munib Veiz (redacted) (redacted). So that is one of the main reasons why I remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did any other detainee disappear in that same manner -- oh, wait a second. Did you ever see them again or hear of them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Whom do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I mean these five people you have just talked about. Did you ever hear of them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know. That question seems somewhat out of place, really. How can I see men whom I saw being killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The bodies were never found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Perhaps they will never be found like many others, hundreds and hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that the question could be asked in a slightly different way, perhaps explaining to the witness that whilst he believes they were dead, you have to prove that they were dead and you want to know whether he ever saw them anywhere in any form again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, you heard His Honour speak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I heard, I did hear. Unfortunately, my answer is no. I wish I could see them alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall if any other detainees from your room were taken away before these five and had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. A day before that, on the 24th, that was practically the first time that people were taken from my room that I registered. On the 24th, Kruno Marinovic; Elvedin Cedic, Ekinda; Refik Cankusic, called Pepi; and a young man, Alija Altoka. I know his father was an electrician.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person Elvedin "Ekinda" Cedic, did he also have the nickname Enko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Ekinda was his name -- Cedic, his last name, Elvedin, his first name, and Ekinda, his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the list this person is listed as number 5, but it says here "Enko Cedic," and we think this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, who took these four out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Boban Pejic. Slobodan Pejic, Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After they were taken, did you hear the sounds of beatings again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. They went to the administrative part of the building and I never saw them again. They did not come back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of them again or hear of them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
