utterances.text: Was someone taken out from your room after this incident with your relative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Nail Hodzic, on the 26th, in the evening hours again. You're going to ask me if I saw him again. No, I never saw him again, and he never came back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he taken away in a group of people from other rooms as well, or was he taken alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He went to the administrative part of the building on his own. He had to pass there. I don't know where he went, but he went to the administrative part of the building alone. And it was again in the evening, perhaps around 10.00 or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of beating after he had left Room 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Hodzic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know he was a driver all his professional life. I don't know if he did anything else. He was a driver by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall if anyone else was taken out later? Do you recall any particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th of June, a large group of people were taken away. I believe it was 37, if my memory serves me properly, and I knew some of them. They were taken out of the compound and none of them ever returned either. Nurko Nisic, a former policeman, was one of them; Mate Ivancic, a male nurse, a Catholic, a Croat; Zulfo Veiz; Fuad Mandzo; two Soro brothers. And I can't really go on. Perhaps I could remember a couple of names more, but it would take a lot of time. You must know that it happened seven and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the 28th of June --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: What I have just told you happened on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you hear beatings, the sound of beatings when these 37 were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. They did not stay there. They were taken away somewhere, but where ... I mean, they were not kept there because they were a large group of people. It was a large number, 37, as far as I could count. I believe there were 37. Perhaps one or two -- perhaps plus one or two -- plus or minus one or two, but that was roughly the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they taken out in a big group all together or were they taken out in separate smaller groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Gathered together. They all left together. They all went together through that passage that I've already shown, through that part of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Schedule C list. That is Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you mind moving closer to the microphones? The translators are having difficulty hearing you. Would you move your chair in closer to the microphones. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned many of the persons listed on the schedule, so we do not need to repeat their fate, but I would like to ask you about some people you have not yet mentioned, if you can tell us anything about them. That is, number 2 on the list, Salem Bico. Do you know him and do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, do I know him. He was a policeman too. Whether retired or not, I don't know. He was a policeman in Foca. And as for what happened to him, well, lots of things happened to him. For a long time he was isolated somewhere on the ground floor. He and another one nicknamed Sporna Selimovic [phoen], I think. They spent there a long time, and after that they did not turn up in the camp again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. But he was there for a long time, and he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you recall when you saw him for the last time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next person, number 3, Abdurahman Cankusic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The next person, number 3, is Abdurahman Cankusic, brother of Refik Cankusic. And I think that on the 13th of July, with Adil Krajcin and one of the Soros, a big guy and an electrician, sometime around the 13th of July they were taken away in the afternoon and did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the person 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. And 24 you have Seval Soro. Under 24, Seval Soro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the person 6, Juso Dzamalija. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I personally know him. He's an elderly man. He worked in a shop. I did not see him in the camp. However, one of the guards told me that he hanged himself in one of the neighbouring rooms which was there for correction. I don't know whether it was a solitary confinement cell or not, but I was just told that they found him one morning and that he had hanged himself before that. One of the guards told me that, and I'm not going to mention his name. I would mention that man with pride, but I don't want him to have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you mean a guard who helped you, who was correct to you? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I believe that he was a very fair person and a gleam of light in all this time that I spent there. A human being with utmost dignity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let's now move on to the person number 8, Ramo Dzendusic. What can you tell about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I saw Ramo Dzendusic in the camp. He was not in my room. I saw him for some time and then he was taken away. But I don't know by who or where or when exactly. After that, he was nowhere to be seen in the camp. Who took him, where, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 9, Adil Granov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, Adil Granov. An engineer who worked in Zica. For some time he was in my room. I can't remember who took him away and where, but I think that he was taken away with a few other men. I can't remember this very well. He spent some time in our room. A quiet man like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And number 12, Esad Kiselica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Esad Kiselica is an electrician, I know that. And I know his father. He was not in my room, although I would see him from the window and in passing when we went to the restaurant. He was not in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he disappear from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He disappeared from the KP Dom. He was there for some time and then he did not appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 13, Halim Konjo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Number 13, Halim Konjo. He had a private catering establishment. Son of Ahmed Konjo and his mother Nusa. I don't know about him from before he was in the camp, but I found out -- I don't know whether I should mention the name. I found out from a man who Milorad Krnojelac told that he had found him dead one morning in his office, that he died as a result of beatings. Now, should I name this person or not? It is really up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, you can name this person who told you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It is Rasim Jusufovic, a colleague, a former colleague of Milorad Krnojelac. They used to work together in a school.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: What did I say? Did I say Rasim Kiselica? What did I say, Jusufovic? It's Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You said Jusufovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Then it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did Mr. Jusufovic tell you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: On the 31st of August, 1992, since he was deported with me to the town of Rozaje in Montenegro, together with 35 other inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did Mr. Jusufovic tell you about his conversation with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, he told me, among other things, what I told you now about Konjo, and he also told me that Krnojelac had said to him, "Well, had I known yesterday that this would happen -- had I known what would be happening, I wish I could have died a day before that." I mean, he was referring to the day before he became what he became.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And let's move on in the list. You have already mentioned Adil Krajcin. Therefore, we go now to number 18, Omer Mujezinovic. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know the name of Omer Mujezinovic. I knew a man called Omer Mujezinovic, but I think that he was killed in a car accident a lot before the war broke out. So I don't really know the name of Omer Mujezinovic in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you look at the numbers 21 to 23, you have several Rikalos listed. What can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: These are three brothers. I don't know which order you've put, but the one under number 21 is the oldest. I know that. He's an electrician. And now as far as 22 and 23 are concerned, they're brothers too. All three are brothers. But I don't know out of these remaining two which one is the middle one and which is the youngest one. One of them went on the 28th of June in that big group and the other one remain. I don't know which one is the younger one and which one is the older one out of these two. I just know that they were Rikalos and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And all three of them disappeared or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know about the middle one. One of them remained. I don't know which one it was. I don't know what happened to him. And 29 was in this group, Veiz Zulfo, unless I've mentioned him already; Nurko Nisic, all these names I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have not yet mentioned the person number 25, Kemal Tulek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know who that is. I know he was in the camp. But he was not with me in my room. He was not with me in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have already mentioned Mr. Dzemal Vahida, and you have described to us that he was beaten on several occasions. When did you see him for the last time in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I saw him the last time on the 28th of June. He was also in this group. Dzemal Vahida is also a policeman. He also left in this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have described to us and you have pointed out to us the room where you actually saw beatings happen. Could you hear the sound of beating or screaming from other parts of the administration building while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In this part that is in front of us, specifically Enes Uzunovic, he would be moaning so badly when he was beaten. I don't even know how to express myself. He sounded like an animal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was a different one. Did you hear beatings from other parts of the administration building other than the part you have pointed out to us already on the photos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I could not hear. I did not hear. I only heard from the entrance and around the entrance because that was nearby. I could not hear from over there where the windows were closed. I mean, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. How did these beatings and this screaming affect you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It created a nervousness psychologically. Well, it is psychological. You know, every normal person is afraid for his own life. If you see that the person next to you was taken away, beaten up, and you're expecting to be the next one, you can imagine what it was like. It was awful; it was terrible; it was so sad; it was murderous.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides these beatings you have described to us, did you ever see a detainee being beaten in the yard or in the canteen or on the way to the canteen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, there were slaps, slight kicks or slight blows with a hand. But anything that would be prepared specifically, well, no. I mean, you'd walk by and he'd hit you or kick you, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "he," who do you mean? Anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The guard. Any guard. Perhaps there are only a few honourable exceptions; one man for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were detainees taken out for exchanges while you were there, before you were taken, actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They were taken out. All were taken out, in fact, under the pretext of being taken away for exchanges. Perhaps they never got there. Nobody was ever told that they were being taken out to be liquidated. Everybody was taken out -- I mean, these people would look very happy, they would be pleased to be going to be exchanged, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many detainees were taken out for exchange before you were exchanged? Do you recall the number, the approximate number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I mean, I can't remember. Quite a few were taken away, for sure. In August, quite a lot of men were taken out in groups; sometimes 10, sometimes 15 or 20. I did not keep any statistics; I mean, even in normal circumstances, I'm not a statistics expert so I would not keep statistical records. But I just know ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see these detainees later on or did some of them disappear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I never saw any of these men who were taken away before I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross come to the KP Dom while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, once. I can't remember the date exactly when this happened. A woman came from the International Red Cross with an interpreter. I think it was a young girl from Foca; I did not recognise her but these younger ones did. She was a young girl. As soon as the woman walked in, Slavko Koroman showed up and said, "You can't put any questions. You can't talk here. There is Serb authority here. We are here to approve what will be discussed and what will not be discussed." Outside there was a group of journalists, photographers, whatever there might have been. They didn't let them come in. They were between those two buildings, the area that I said looked like a park. They gave some cigarettes to those people, those inmates, who were at windows. So they didn't really complete the job they had set out to complete. They had never come again until I was released on the 30th of August. So I was not even registered as an inmate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Koroman, who was that? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not anyone who could give orders to Koroman, or I was not his employer. He was there all the time. He was a former guard in the KP Dom. I think he was a retiree. He lived near me. I don't know about these details, whether he had retired or not, but the fact remains that he was in the camp all the time. On one occasion I talked to him a bit. Actually, on that day I was taken to the transfusion department in hospital because I wanted to give blood for a man who needed blood. I had a blood group, B negative, which was very rare; at least in Foca it was rare. So I gave blood for this person. And then when I returned, I saw Koroman in the compound. He was taking Sacir Smajkan, holding him under the arm. He was a judge, this Sacir Smajkan, as far as I can remember. His T-shirt was bloody around the neck; he was barefoot, dirty. He was a sight to behold. He looked awful. When he put him up there, I was standing in front of the restaurant and he said, "What's up?" and I said, "Well, I had been giving blood and now I'm waiting for the people from my room to come so that we can go and have lunch in the restaurant, and I want to take advantage of the sunshine now." He said to me, "Go into the shade a bit. You won't feel well," and I said, "What happened to Sacir?" and he said, "Well, leave this full alone. He got drunk. Look what he looks like." Afterwards I heard a completely different story. Sacir said that he was beaten up and then brought in the way he looked then and handed over to Koroman in the camp. That's what I know. I don't know any other details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said you donated blood. Did you do that voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I mean, you can treat it any way you want to now. I did not refuse it; I gave it voluntarily. But then can you understand what would have happened to me if I said a resolute no? I mean, I don't even know myself what would have happened to me. But I didn't want anything bad to happen to me, so as a precaution I agreed to donate blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean you were asked specifically to donate blood because of your rare blood group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that way. I don't know exactly who came to the door of our room and said, "Who has blood group B negative?" And then perhaps because I was afraid or whatever, I felt as if he were looking at me, as if he had fixed his gaze on me, so what else could I have done but said that I had that group? He drove me to hospital. There was another former inmate there of Serb ethnicity. Rade Baralic, I think his name was, from Banja Luka, from somewhere around Banja Luka. He also donated blood together with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's talk about the camp commander. Who was the warden of the camp during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I repeat once again: I'm only talking about the period that I spent in the camp. As for everything that was before that or after that, I'm not going to talk about that and I don't want to talk about that. While I was in the camp, the warden was Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know this? How did you get this information that he was the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I got this information -- I mean, I saw the man a few times, perhaps five or six times, as he was passing from the administrative building. Also there were his security people, and he wore an officer's uniform. I mean, it was no secret. His guards knew; those who were subordinated to him, they knew who their warden was. I mean, it's not any secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But who told you? Did the guards tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: A guard told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honours, I think that first he should be asked whether somebody had told him, and only then, who, and not putting this kind of leading question, "Who was it who told you this? Was it a guard?" It is a leading question. I think that first he should be asked whether anybody told him, who told him, and so on. The question contains an answer that is actually being elicited from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think your point is a good one, Mr. Bakrac, but may I remind you again: It's not made better by repeating it twice. He hasn't actually said that he was told by the guards. What he has said was, "I got this information," and then he doesn't go on to explain from where; and then some lines later, he says, "His guards knew; those who were subordinated to him ..." Now, you have drawn the conclusion that he had been told by the guards, but he really should give that evidence himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So how did you get the information that he was the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I got this information -- I mean, it wasn't only I; everybody, we all got this information. After all, I mean, certain guards -- well, again, I'm saying I don't want to mention specific names. But we had pretty good contacts with some of the guards. I'm saying there were not very many of them, but there were some. Some would even give us cigarettes. Somebody was friends with one of them; some with the other. But I think that the real information is from the very opening of the camp, and I think it was precisely the guards who were saying this. And then as things developed, it was then established that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also hear from inmates, from other inmates that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. Everybody. There's not a single detainee, a single inmate. I'm claiming that there's not a single one who had spent any amount of time in the camp without knowing who the warden was. It's absurd to ask that. But then, of course, this is a court, so the truth has to be established. And it's not for me to judge. It's up to me to say what I know, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And did you know Mr. Krnojelac from before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him as the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know, but probably the ruling party. I don't know who. Probably the SDS. Who else would? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I know -- I know even in normal circumstances that a ruling party appoints persons to certain responsible posts. They don't appoint someone from a different party or somebody who is not a member of any party. That is my assumption. That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Krnojelac had a position in the SDS; that he was a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I was not a member of the SDS or the SDA. I don't know how many there were. I was not a member of any party, so I cannot make any claims. I mean, I could only guess. But I guess, I guess, that he was a supporter of that party. I don't know. I'm not making any claims. Let me be quite clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said that you saw him several times. When did you see him? What time of the day was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: During the day. During the day. During the course of the day. Not during the night. During the day, within the compound. I would see him over there, for example, towards the restaurant or as he was going to the administrative building. Then there was always someone with him. Probably his subordinates, security people or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: An olive-green/grey officer's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And could you see if he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Perhaps a pistol but not any big weapons. He didn't have any big weapons in his hands like an automatic rifle when I saw him. I'm telling you about what I saw and about the time when I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And speaking of Mr. Krnojelac, is this the accused here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me put to you at this point what the accused himself says about his position. He said that the KP Dom, during the war, had two separate sections, a military part and a civilian part. The Muslim detainees were in the military part and the normal convicts were in the civil part, and he had nothing to do with the military part. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly, Muslim detainees were in the military part, in the military part of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Krnojelac claims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: For goodness sake. I'm a Muslim. I was there. Where was I taken prisoner? What kind of a soldier was I? What kind of a soldier was a 14-year-old boy? What kind of a soldier was an 84-year-old man? I think it's not true, and such things simply do not hold.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Krnojelac doesn't claim that you were a prisoner of war, he only says the Muslims were kept in a military part that he had no dealings with. What I would like to know from you is was there this division, a division between a military part and a civilian part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. No. I state with full responsibility that there were not any military prisoners while I was in the camp. While I was in the camp, I repeat, no military was brought into the camp nor were there any military persons there. All of these persons were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned Mr. Todovic. When you saw him in the prison, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Are you talking about his clothes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He had military olive-green/grey uniform on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did not see one, really. I mean, I don't remember seeing one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Todovic behave towards the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I said already. He assigned me to work and then, as far as I'm concerned, I didn't have any other contacts with him. What happened happened after working in the kitchen for three days, and I went to solitary confinement, and after back to my Room 11. Well, for the most part, appointed people -- I mean, I think his role was to assign people to various kinds of work, I mean, convicts and inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: On the 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many detainees were released with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: In the first attempt there were 55 men on the bus, but that bus got as far as Niksic, roughly, and a white Golf intercepted the bus. The bus stopped. Pero Elez then came onto the bus, looked around, look around, and told the driver to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you briefly. Pero Elez, who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, Pero Elez was another of the former guards in KP Dom, as far as I know, and who had been retired because of poor nerves or something. I did not see him either on the eve of the war or during the war or that -- I am told he was a Chetnik leader, but whether it's true or not, I don't know, but he must have been something if he had the authority to tell the bus with inmates to turn back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was this in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue with your narrative. What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, that bus went back and that car was in front of us and took us to the KP Dom. Meanwhile, he disappeared somewhere and we went back into the KP Dom. To repeat, it was 55 men. After we came back, they put us again in Room 11, that blasted Room 11 once again, but there was nobody else there. They must have distributed the others in other rooms to replenish them, but there was nobody there. Some 10 minutes or so later, Bozo Pejic comes with a list of paper and calls out 20 names out of those 55 men, and says, "Get ready quickly. You're to be exchanged." That's how it was. He took them away and -- and the 35 of us stayed behind. Then again, after some 10, 15, 20 minutes, more or less - doesn't matter - we were told to get ready and go. So we went down to the administrative building and then out. There was a bus parked. And once again, Savo Todovic turned up again, called out our names. We got onto the bus. He drew out our attention that the bus had curtains inside, drew our attention -- warned us not to look through the windows or else something bad might happen. And we were driven away. We were taken away along the same route, and sometime in the evening hours, the night had already fallen, we arrived to Scepan Polje, which is the boundary between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the drivers then -- the bus drivers then went to a wooden shed which I suppose was the border authority or something, with that list of ours names, and uniformed individuals in military uniforms then came onto the bus, beat us - I suppose we shall be suffering the effects of that to the end of our lives - with automatic rifle butts, on the backs, all over the body, and there was about half an hour of that ill-treatment and they got off. And the drivers came back with the list in their hands and we went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you here. You said that 20 persons were singled out from your group as it was in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of people were singled out? Did they have anything in common?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I wouldn't say anything. It was just like that. Or perhaps somebody knew those men for some reason. I mean, I don't know. I don't see anything there. There were two very old men. One was 84 and one 60-something. But there were very young, in their 20s. So that -- I don't think anything -- there's anything that I might think that they were taken, singled out on the basis of some plan or something. Their names were just taken from the list. Why? I couldn't really ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to these people? Did you ever see any of them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No, not -- unfortunately, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you meet your family again and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, you see that bus -- when you interrupted me -- so we went on with that bus. And in the morning, at daybreak or somewhere around 7.00, 6.00, half past six thereabouts, Niksic, Titograd, Ivangrad called now Baronave [phoen], to a place called Rozaje. And slightly before Rozaje, we sort of were to go to Macedonia, and that is what Savo Todovic had said. But somewhere along the way between Baronave and Rozaje, Kunarac, the driver, because we knew one another, and he sort of showed to me to come to him, and I did so. And he said, "I really don't know. I don't think that Macedonia will take you in. The best thing would be for me to leave you in Rozaje, because the Muslims are a majority then." And so I said, "Well, do that. So leave us wherever." And that's how it was. The bus terminal in Rozaje, we stopped and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not need all the details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I was saying it because that is where I found my wife, who had arrived with a convoy -- left for Foca with a convoy 14 days before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And you have already told us about your weight loss, and you have told us about your injuries you received during the beating. Did you suffer any permanent physical consequences as a result of the conditions or your beating in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, my mental health, psychologically, I'm not all right. And often -- now I know what my brother's name is, now I simply can't remember it. Yes, of course, there are consequences, but one has to live and go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What consequences? Do you mean -- these psychological consequences, what are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I have trouble sleeping; it's very seldom that I sleep more than two hours a night. I shake; my hands sweat; I'm very nervous.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First, let me introduce myself to the witness and tell him that my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and to wish him a good day. I represent here the accused Milorad Krnojelac. Good afternoon to you. In the beginning of your testimony, Witness, when asked by the Prosecutor, you said that in your building, some four or five Serbs had stayed in your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you also said that Donje Polje was an area which was mostly Muslim, what was the ethnic ratio in your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think -- well, I need a little time to -- I believe it was half/half. There were 29 apartments, and there were 14 of one and 15 of the other, so I believe something like that. I do not know, but I think it was fairly -- fairly balanced, fairly even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I point out that when you are both speaking the same language, you must pause before the answer is given and before the next question is asked so that the translators can keep up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, will you be so kind and tell me if you remember an SDA rally in Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that rally in Foca. Do I remember it. And (redacted), that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people attended the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I haven't finished my answer yet. I can tell you that I did not attend the rally, and at that time I was in my summer cottage, which is about 10 kilometres from my home. Believe me, if you mean my political option, I had none. I did not support any party, I never supported any party, and I am a peace-minded -- a passivist. So believe me, I did not attend it. I heard that very many people were there, that there was a rally and that very many people were there, but I was not present, neither I nor my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to be clear. I wasn't trying to intimate by my question that that was what I was driving at, whether you were a member. I do not doubt what you have just told us. What I want to know - and you have answered it in part, that you heard that very many people had been there - will you agree with me that it was said between 100.000 and 150.000, that is, those are the figures in the press and the rumour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know only as much as you do. From the press, yes, the figure of 100.000 was mentioned, but I did not see them. I mean, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if, in the statement that you made to the Prosecutor's Office in 1995, you spoke about the SDS rally which brought together 10.000 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Again, I do not know how many people. Again, I can tell you that I wasn't there. It was in the football stadium. I know of the Sutjeska Club; that is what I do know. But again I was not there. I repeat: I was away. Because those rallies usually took place over the weekend, so that again I was out in my summer cottage and I wasn't in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I agree. But I'm asking if it is correct that you said, "I heard that there were some 10.000 people present"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so, I guess so. I don't remember anymore at all. You must know that it was a long time ago and I am of an advanced age. I may have said that I heard that. Just as I heard that there were about 100.000 at that other rally, I may have heard that there were 10.000 at this one. But I wasn't at either of them, and you cannot say that I was present at a rally and I counted all those people present. That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Precisely, that is what I said, Witness. I did not say that you were there but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know what you said. I know what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in that statement you said that all the trouble started because of the aspiration of Serbs to come together, to be united in one state, and that includes that rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Rally -- as a rally, I exclude, but I know what I heard around cafeterias and shops or at work. And even with my closest friends, I would have an argument. All Serbs in one state, that was the proclamation of the Serb Democratic Party, and you have to grant that. Well, you don't have to, but that was the proclamation of the Serb Democratic Party, of the SDS. So I'm not trying to underestimate, to understate, the proclamations of other parties, I'm not trying to do that, because I should say that on either side there were as many such things as you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. I'm trying to speed things up because I have a few questions on this subject, and I know how the Court wishes to learn about this subject. But certain things are important to me, and I'm simply trying to cut the answers short, just bearing in mind the time. I hope this is not being misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may get shorter answers if you ask different questions, if I may suggest that. But this business about the political rallies, surely, is of very minor importance. Whether there was an attack upon one or more civilian populations doesn't really matter. The Prosecution only has to prove that there was at least one, and the fact that there may have been an attack upon the Serb civilian population by the Muslims doesn't seem to affect that. So could we get on to what really is in issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand this perfectly, but I think that the Prosecution also went into that. But I won't waste too much time. I only have two questions more on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So in line with what you just told us, didn't the Serbs already live in one state in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So why would they need another state, since they already had one state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in any political organisation so don't ask me that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, my last question on the subject: In your view, in the area where the population distribution was roughly 50/50 and at a meeting of one ethnically-oriented party we have 100.000, 150.000, and the other one is attended by 10.000 people, doesn't that represent real grounds for fear of that side which could bring together only 10.000 people at a rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Sir, this is again a political issue and I'm not a politically-minded person. Thank you for asking me those questions, and they are quite decent questions, but please don't try to embroil, to involve me in politics because I have nothing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you. I shall move on to some specific matters that you mentioned in your testimony. Is it true that in your statement you told the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, on the 4th and 5th September of 1995 -- that you made a statement to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you make this statement of your own volition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal you gave yet another statement on the 14th of November, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it may be a small point but it is an important one: The investigators are not the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, they are the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, which is completely independent of the Tribunal. It may be different in other countries, but in the system we work under, there is no relationship between the Prosecution and the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My apologies. The legal system that I come from is somewhat different; hence, this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you made both those statements of your own free will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So will you please explain: Did you, in 1995, remember better -- did you have a better recollection of the events in 1995 than in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Of course, 100 per cent. And I'm sure that this year I don't know what I knew in 1998. Senility, I think, is a natural phenomenon so that that's how things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Then how do you explain that -- I'm referring to the incident which, to say the least, was very unpleasant to you, that is, the incident of the 26th of June --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think it was the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, the 25th. That about the incident of the 25th of June which happened in the evening hours - you said about 10.00, half past - how is it possible that then, in 1995 - now you tell us that you remember that event best - how is it that, in 1995, you told the investigators of the Prosecutor's Office that what you saw was an incident which had taken place in the passage of the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Sir, that part of the administrative building is all passage to me, that ground floor, and windows also are part of that, because I went through that passage four or five times. Once I entered; secondly, I went for a visit; that is, when my wife came to visit me, I was again there and I had a guard standing beside me. And that did not look like an office to me. Once, when I went to load flour, I also went through it, and twice as they were escorting us through, and it simply looked like a passage to me. It doesn't look like a room, like a furnished room. It simply looked like a passage. I think that is the only misunderstanding. There can be no other misunderstanding about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor's investigators show you the photographs when you were giving them your second statement on the 4th and 5th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your second statement you said: "When I said in my previous statement that the murder happened in a passage, that was an error. The passage had a door so it would be impossible to see through once the door was closed."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, you see, there must be some misunderstanding. It wasn't through this door because my position was not such to watch through the door. I would have to be in that passage to watch through the door, and I was watching it through the window of my room, which was number 11. So I couldn't look around the corner through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is clear when you tell us so, but in 1995 you said something different.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, it must have been a misunderstanding, whether it was a translation or what. But you must believe me when I say that I saw what I watched through the window. I could not watch it from the other side. I watched it directly through the window, just as I look now. I could not look through the door. You saw the photograph, I remember it well, and that slightly protruding part, it is not frontal at all. So I couldn't look through the door even if I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I know you couldn't. But then how could you state in your first statement that you saw that in the passage, and that it was only in 1998 that you realised it was impossible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: That passage, I've already explained it to you. It just looks as one piece. That is how I see it; that is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do I understand you well when you say that that window, which you identified, of the room which you identified today, that you define it as the passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: That is how it looks to me, because I did not go into it. But what I could see through the window with the broken glass and with lights on, I saw it. To my mind, it was something like a passage, because there were no desks or anything where those people were beaten and killed there. I don't know if you're trying to provoke me or what.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will, please, counsel and the witness make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are being asked to pause. It's very difficult for us to interrupt you all the time, but almost since I last warned you, you have been starting the question before the translation is finished. Now, I'm not suggesting you should listen to a translation to confuse you, but you can probably hear in your earphones that there is a translation going on, and please just wait for the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise once again. The effect of cross-examination is lost through interpretation, but that is nobody's fault, but I apologise. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you want us to hear what's going on, I'm afraid you're also going to have to lose that advantage. But I assure you that cross-examination can be stopped even if you -- if we're all understanding the same language if you start to shout the witness down, and that's what it sounds like to us. So please just pause. We'll all get on a lot better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, did I understand what you said? If I did, you said that that room was empty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there was something on the floor, some small things, but it looked empty to me. Looking from my window in its far right corner was that -- I don't know what it was. There was a tool of a kind. Again, I say I don't know what it was. Perhaps it was something to do with the electric power, with electricity. I don't know. But there were red lights. Red lights could be seen when other lights would be out. So there was some instrument, some device of a kind, something. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But that device, you did not mention it in either your first or your second statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not. I don't know why I didn't. I suppose I wasn't asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But this is purely for information's sake, for you, because you say -- you said -- you said that it was empty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, there was something in that corner, but it wasn't really particularly conspicuous, and you couldn't really see any tables, any desks or anything from Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But could you judge what it was? What kind of a device was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I suppose some control board perhaps. Perhaps power control panel or something. I don't really know. I don't think a device. I don't think it was a machine. It was an apparatus or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But do you think it could have been a telephone switchboard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. Could have been. Could be perhaps. It simply did not cross my mind. It didn't occur to me, but, yes, it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is 1.00. I have a few more questions, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. We'll take the break. You've been giving the translators a very bad time. We'll resume again at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we talked about the premises where these unfortunate incidents occurred, and you said that you allow for the possibility that the devices you saw were a telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Witness, could you move up closer to the table again so that the translators can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you repeated that on that table there was a small lamp, a little light. Were those little lights on when you looked from the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I can't remember. The light was on in the room, and it would probably be more obvious to me than when the room was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that from your window you could see these lamps turned off? How big are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, about as big as these buttons here in front of me on the video monitor, the computer monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you managed to see that from the room that you were watching all of this from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Only when they were on. Only when they were on. When there is no light during the night you could see these little red lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on the critical evening when you were watching, the light was not on in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: On the critical night, the light was on in the room. If you are referring to the night when --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The one that's mentioned, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: It was on. The light was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Although the light was on, you saw that these little lamps were on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. No. When I say the little lamps were on, I could see that all the time, for months while I was there, when the lights were not on. And I think that this has nothing to do with the incident that I talked about. Perhaps I mentioned this just in passing, just tentatively. I think that these little lamps have nothing to do with the incident. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you mention these little lamps so that you would identify the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How big a part of this room that we are discussing now could you see from your window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, let's say viewed from the window, more than a half of this other -- this other half of the room. For example, if I'm looking from here now, I can see, say, from my table here to that table there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. The half from the window to the middle of the room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. More than a half, because my room was higher up, if you look at the configuration of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you are saying this now, is it correct that when you spoke to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that the persons were lined up against the wall opposite the window of that room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Facing the wall, their backs turned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How could you see this since only a minute ago you said that you could see only half, a bit more than half of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think that this is a bit provocative. It is the part of the room that can be seen. So it is the opposite half, the other half. They had their backs turned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you said, and you confirmed now, that they lined them up against a wall, that is, opposite the wall where the window was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you said that from the position you were watching, you could see up to half of the room or a bit more than half of the room, the half and a bit more than half of this room from the window to the middle of the room. Then I'm asking you: How could you see the persons who were lined up against the opposite wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I cannot understand what kind of confusion this is. I think it's quite simple. If you see part of what you see in front of you, the middle, then you can see the people who are lined up against the wall over there. I think that's quite clear, clear as daylight. Why is this misunderstanding there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm not suggesting you must accept what he has said, but he has said very clearly that the half of the room which he could see was the far half. Now, it's no good asking him the same question all the time. You may challenge that if you wish, but that's what he said, and, if I may say so, he said it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether there's a mistake in the translation. It was my understanding, on the basis of what was interpreted, on the basis of what you said, that he saw the further half of the room, the one that was further away from the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is right, and that is where they were lined up against the wall. Now, as I say, you don't have to accept his statement, but that's what he has said. So it's no good asking him the same question each time to produce the same result.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the witness see these persons or, rather, did he see where the guards were in relation to these detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: They were facing these men and they had their backs turned to the window. Before that they physically mistreated them. There was general commotion. That is my position. Those men were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the guards had their backs turned to the window.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think that things are getting complicated. I mean, in this room, is somebody turned half left, half right? It is enough to say that somebody was in this room. Now, whether he's turned half left, half right, I don't know, it's of no consequence to me. But then I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that there were five prisoners in the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Of course there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many guards were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Those that were mentioned and perhaps some I could not remember. Again, I'm saying I did not keep statistical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you give me the number? You said those mentioned and others. Just give me the number of guards who were present.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I can't tell you how many. Five or six or seven, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Five or six men for sure. But all of this is an approximation, sir. Again, I'm saying I was not there as a statistics expert who was keeping records. I was a man who was -- well, I don't have to explain this to you. You know this full well. And the fact that I am so particularly affected by this detail in the camp is quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm truly sorry about that, but I do have the right to put questions to you, and I do hope I'm trying to do this as decently as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Go ahead and ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see some weapons in the guards' hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I think they had pistols, not longer firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "I think," does that mean that you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you viewed this incident from Room 11 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: From a part of that room which is on the left-hand side in relation to the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: If you are looking from the administrative part of the building, then it is on the right-hand side; if you are looking at the building where Room 11 is, then it's the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any beds in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where did the prisoners sleep? I mean, in the room that you were looking from, from where you were observing this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, yes. But I thought you were asking me about the room where this incident occurred. There were beds in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any beds, bunkbeds, the way we saw them on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Wire beds or, rather, metal beds as we used to have in the army, made of metal and then there was this metal net, mesh, underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were these beds next to the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, they -- the beds were put wherever it suited people, this way or that way. There wasn't any rule or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself, who else observed this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I could give you 20 names for sure. Muhamed Lisica, one of them for sure, and the two Soro brothers, Esad and his younger brother, 14 or 15 years old. Esad Soro. Then there was Rasim Merkez, Muharem Merhabovic. Lots; over 30 men. Muhamed Lisica was next to me for sure, and Rasim from Josanica. I said the name just now. Merkez. Merkez. Muharem Bacvic and many others, many other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that all 20 of you viewed these events from the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: As I said, not all 20 of us could watch, but I was watching, Muhamed Lisica was watching, Rasim was watching also, and two on the side. The lights were out, and our heads were on the windows, on the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that there was a lot of rain that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was raining very hard, especially at that moment. Perhaps it started half an hour before that. It was raining very, very hard outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were the windows closed in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: No. No. The glass was broken on that window. How and why and when, I have no idea. If that glass was not broken, one could not see that much. Perhaps we could not see any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the other windows at that level -- actually, were the other windows at that level painted with white paint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Not over there. They were not painted over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having said before the break that you saw a guard walking upstairs and carrying blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Zoka Matovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You saw him on the stairs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, from that room you can see the stairs that are slanted and that lead to the next floor. I was not in that room, so could I not say what the ceiling was like, but you can see the stairs that go further up very nicely, and also that he was on those stairs and carrying a few blankets, olive-green/grey. He was carrying them on his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The window from which one can see the stairs, is that right next to the window that you were watching?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I cannot decipher which window you are referring to, but from the opening, you could see -- I mean, through the window you could see the man going upstairs and carrying the blankets over his arm. I mean, I'm not an expert. I cannot say whether you could see it from this window or that window, but you could see the man carrying these blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am only interested in having you tell me which window this is in relation to the window that you identified as the window through which you watched this event. From which side and whether it's the first or second window or whatever. If you could do this without the assistance of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I could not say, but it could be seen -- it could be seen when he went up. You could see the stairs and also when he was going up, and you could see the slant. That is the truth. And now whether it is that window or the one next to it, but at any rate, it was slanted and he was walking up from one room to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Witness, may I remind you, please pause before the answer. I know you are very involved in this, but for us to get on, the translators have to have that pause. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement given to the investigators of the OTP, did you say that every detention building had a series of solitary confinement cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I know, I mean, about my part, but two buildings are linked. I know that there were solitary confinement cells underneath the stairs. I don't know whether there's one or two, but that's where that man hanged himself, the one I mentioned. Also, there were some beatings there and things like that. And then on the other hand, there are those other solitary confinement cells. I mean, this is a big compound and all the buildings are attached. It's not that there are any detached buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said now that in your part - let's call it A or an inverted "F".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: The entire complex of buildings looks like an inverted "F".

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm saying that in the part that you were in, you said that there were solitary confinement cells.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Not in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, not in your room but in that part of your building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, in that part of the building that goes this way and then that way and then to the right and then there are these stairs and then underneath those stairs there were these rooms that was solitary confinement or whatever, but I know that people were staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Today, in response to the Prosecutor's question, you said and you showed solitary confinement cells in part of building B on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is where I was, and there is a larger number of solitary confine cells there, but I don't know how many people this particular one can take, but I know Asif Cajnovic [phoen], after a physical mistreatment that was quite exceptional, spent five or six days there. This was one of these physical mistreatments. He spent some time to recuperate and then he was thrown in. And then this little Sabovac -- I know him. Everybody knows him. All of Foca knows him. Then he was -- was screaming there as if Wolves were slaughtering him. And then in that solitary confinement cell, the man I mentioned a few minutes ago hanged himself. I can't remember his name now. The man who worked in the shop. Those are facts. Whoever got in there once knew what was there. But I don't know what it looked like inside that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said in your statement, the one that I already mentioned, that had you not made this mistake with the bread, you would have been in the working room as well. Does that mean that that would have been a benefit for you and that you had lost it because of the mistake with the bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, probably the man assigned me to work there. I probably would have remained there otherwise. Probably this was taken as a mistake on my part. I don't know what. I don't know. That is why I was taken to solitary confinement where I was beaten up. Whether I would have remained there or not, well, maybe I would have remained. I don't know. I don't know what would have happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the KP Dom at the time while you were staying there, were there any Serb persons who were already serving their time there, who had been sentenced before, earlier on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. I know two of them, but they were at the well-known Focanski Brioni, where they had the farm there. Actually, I came to the camp before they did. They came but they did not stay there. They were around the food during the first days, that little Rade Baralic, who donated blood when I did, and another young man. I never registered his name or surname, nor did I have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your statement you said that there were such persons, to the best of your knowledge, that there were 10 or 15 such persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Well, I think there were. As a matter of fact, I don't know whether I mentioned this, one of them was ill, he had tuberculosis. He had a separate dish where they put his food so that others would not use the same dish. He was a very old person who was in prison before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have to put a question to you now which had already been put but was obviously misconceived. Part of the defence of the accused was quoted: that the KP Dom was divided into the civilian and military parts. You said that there were no military prisoners but only civilian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was my answer. That is correct, there weren't any soldiers. I didn't see any; I did not see any such person, any soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since I already mentioned that it is obviously misconceived, that is, that there was a misunderstanding of what the accused stated, the accused did not state that there were soldiers who were detained, but he said that the detained Muslims were within the zone of responsibility of the military.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know any such persons. The persons I know -- I mean, I don't know such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. Again you did not understand what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I did understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The prisoners were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: They were not military persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, these prisoners were under the responsibility of the military, of the military command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know under whose responsibility they were. I know where we stayed. I really cannot know who's up there in the command and who is responsible for these men. Now, I did not appoint them, I did not belong there, and I cannot say anything about this, really, as to who ordered who to do what. I mean, as far as this question is concerned, I really know nothing. I mean, I really cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know the name Nedzib Lojo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And Hasan Lojo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Lojo got out with me. He is an elderly man. He was on the bus with me. Nedzib Lojo - I think we did not mention this throughout this case - on the 16th of August, I don't know exactly but I think on the 16th of August, he was taken out of my room. Nedzib Lojo; Serif Hodzic, an elderly man; Resad Hadzimehic; and two brothers, two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. young men, Rustan, I think they are from a settlement near Foca. I don't know where they were taken. Hasan Lojo, if it is that elderly man, I think he is still alive, he got out, if we are talking about the man whom I know as Hasan Lojo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know the name Dzevad Lojo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was he at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know in which room he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Opposite -- I mean, if we were to invert the F, it was opposite. He was not in number 20 with me. It was somewhere there around 20. I don't know which numbers these are, 22, 20, 18, 16. I think that all of them are even numbers. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, would you? My recollection is that the witness had said he didn't want his brother named. I don't know whether that's the one that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His brother's name was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is his brother's name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: His brother's name was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going to show you a statement of a witness who testified, and you are going to give me your comment in relation to this statement. "I remember the 13th of June, 1992 very well because the interrogations lasted all day. Many prisoners from different rooms were taken out for interrogations. From my room, three to four prisoners were taken out. Among them was Zulfo Veiz, who was a policeman in Foca before the arrest, who did not return. And also Mustafa Kuloglija was among the prisoners who were taken out for interrogation on that day."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know about Zulfo Veiz, although I know him; we were born practically in the same village. Mustafa Kuloglija ended up the way I said a few minutes ago. But all of this is not important now. I'm stating with full responsibility that Mustafa Kuloglija, on the 25th of June, 1992, ended up together with Veiz. This really has nothing to do with Zulfo Veiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So what I read out to you is not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's correct or not. I don't know what this person saw. But I know that Mustafa Kuloglija, on the 25th of June, was in the camp. And what happened happened and I said that quite clearly, I think it's as clear as daylight; and what other people said has nothing to do with me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said in your statement -- you said before the break that right before your exchange, 20 persons were taken out and they did not come back, and that you were taken for exchange ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes. We came out right after them. No, I think we do not -- we are not clear. How could we go if it was only ten minutes? Something was, I don't know, not translated properly or something is not clear, because how can I know whether they came back or not? I left ten minutes after them. I did not see them again. I believe somebody asked -- somebody asked if I saw those men again and I said I did not see them again. Whether they returned, I cannot know that because I was already gone from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only one more question for you, Witness. You said in your statement, and again in your testimony today before the break, that when you were leaving for exchange, Savo Todovic delivered a short speech; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
