utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was short. I cannot quote him, but what he said, "Don't look through the windows because something might happen to you." What was the purpose behind it all, I don't know. I wasn't interested; I didn't look. All I saw was what I saw on my way: houses burnt, destroyed mosques, and things. I didn't see much, but that is what I saw. But this is really not important. Let me tell you, I didn't belong to any clan. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question: In your statement to the Prosecution, which you say you gave of your own will, you said about Savo Todovic: "He took decisions by himself with full responsibility." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. At least that is my view, that is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned to us what happened to Mr. Kuloglija on the 25th of June, 1992. Was Mr. Kuloglija only taken out once, and that was on the 25th, or was he taken out several times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: Several times. Before he was taken out and beaten, he had bruises on his face and body. I cannot be more accurate. I cannot give you dates when that happened. I mean, really. And it would be silly for me to keep some statistical record. I don't know when that happened, but it happened several times to this Kuloglija to be taken out for some physical -- physical re-education. He left on the 25th. One cannot say that he did not come back on the 13th of July, because he did come back, but when he left on the 25th, that is when he didn't come back. Again, not at least while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did Mr. Kuloglija tell you what had happened to him when he returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-54
utterances.text: He did not have to say anything. Many people kept silent and said nothing. One could see on them. There were visible signs on them what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask another question? May I ask another additional question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. You've had your opportunity. If it's something that arises out of re-examination, I'm afraid you have no further right to ask any questions. If it is something that you had omitted from your cross-examination and it's something quite different to what is raised in re-examination, you may have leave to ask it, and it too then will become subject to re-examination. But you can't now try to go behind the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely omitted to read the sentence to the end, and it has to do with what I failed to do in the cross-examination and is also related to the question asked in re-examination by my learned friend from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the very sort of thing you can't do, I'm afraid. You cannot now try to cure the answers that have been given in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I understand that, but I also understood that you allowed me to do something that I omitted to do during the cross-examination while I was cross-examining the witness, and I omitted to complete the sentence because I was trying to speed up the examination. That was the only reason. And in that additional sentence -- well, if I'm not allowed to do that, of course I will not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let me see if I can clear it up. Is this the statement that you read to the witness in which a different date was given for when the people were taken out of the room, and you asked him, in effect, "What do you say when somebody else says this was on a different day?" That was the purpose of the cross-examination, was it not? If I may say so, I don't really see how a witness can be asked to say whether somebody else was telling the truth. Does it relate only to the date upon which this other witness says these events occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not the date, the date is the same, but the end of the sentence. Now, I don't know whether I can utter that end of the sentence to show you what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We don't have juries in this jurisdiction. You tell us what the rest of the sentence was and if it does turn out to be something quite separate, then we'll allow you to ask it. But you read it out to us now. I've got what you read out before. It ended up saying, "And Mustafa Kuloglija was among the prisoners who were taken out that day." That's when you finished reading. You will say that wasn't the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Mustafa Kuloglija was also amongst the prisoners who were taken away that day for interrogation and did not return."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, that's what I understood you to be inferring or implying from what you would read. I don't, myself, see that it will take the matter any further. Thank you, Witness. You may leave now, but just wait until the blinds are pulled down on that side of the room so that your identity will not be disclosed to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the next witness is 215, and that witness has no protective measures; is that correct? Ms. Kuo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's correct that we had not previously asked for protective measures, but the witness now wishes to have protective measures and ask leave to request that of this Court. The witness wishes to have a pseudonym as well as the facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's the basis of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness is fearful that if he -- the witness still has property in Foca, and if he ever wishes to return, he may be endangered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not know. I believe I can also voice the opinion of the Defence regarding the application of the Prosecutor. We agreed to the protection measures. However, this witness did not get this property between the Pre-Trial Conference and this date. That reason existed even before that. So why didn't he apply for protective measures at the same time when it was requested for other witnesses? I do not see that as a reason. Perhaps there is some other reason behind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll tell you what the reason behind it is, Mr. Bakrac. It's because having spoken to the Prosecution people here, he has found out that this is available and perhaps even was encouraged to ask for it, which I'm not really certain is proper, but, nevertheless, it seems to be a pattern in these cases. When people arrive here, they suddenly realise -- they hear about television records and television telecasts throughout the whole of Yugoslavia, and it almost inevitably happens when they get here they ask for them. Have you got any doubt that he has this fear about what might happen to him when he returns to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really saw no reason for concern, and all the witnesses that will be coming can be protected or, rather, applications can be made for their protection on those same grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They almost inevitably are. I'm not altogether certain myself how prevalent it is, but it has been the practice of the Tribunal to grant protective measures in those circumstances to both Prosecution and Defence witnesses. And I can assure you that at the moment, I seem to be up to my ears in protective measures applications in another case, and I have read a whole series of reports from the UNHCR and others which detail in quite some measure of detail the problems that people have when they return to one or other of the entities inside Bosnia. It's not limited, I hasten to add, to any one particular entity. And it's not unreasonable to see that there is some concern that they have that they may be mistreated. Now, if you say there is some prejudice to you, I would be very happy to hear it. I'm not sure that you would be able to show any. The only prejudice I see is the fear that these proceedings seem to be conducted more behind closed doors than they should be. Here they will not be conducted behind closed doors. All that will happen is that the screen will remained there, the blinds behind the screen will remain down, about one-third of the public gallery will not be able to see anything inside the courtroom, but, nevertheless, on the screen and through the headphones they'll see and everything that goes on except that they will not see the face of the witness giving evidence. Now, can you tell me what prejudice your client will suffer if we grant these protective measures albeit out of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my objection was mostly on grounds of principle rather than the specific reason. There is this general reason. We think that the witnesses might be much more sincere if their identity were known to everybody. Moreover, the Defence would be able to collect supplementary evidence in view of the identity of those persons, because we also are not at liberty to disclose the names of those persons. The Defence is in a rather unfavourable position, because perhaps somebody, if he knew that that person was testifying or would be testifying, could give us something that would help us to show the -- to undermine the credibility of that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that this witness already had a pseudonym. What is being asked for is the distortion of his face at the time he gives evidence. He would have been referred to throughout as Witness 215, and were you not entitled, under the ordinary protective measures provisions, to disclose that to anybody except in the necessary pursuit of your client's rights in preparing for the trial. So the only thing that is going to be different is that his face will not be seen on television in an undistorted way and, as I say, one-third of the public area will be hidden, out of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the area that I come from, people are recognised, identified, by their faces rather than by their names. But I do not want to waste any more time of the Court. I explained which are the reasons for which we have this objection. I already explained that this is prejudicial to the Defence. I do not have to repeat that. And of course, the Court will decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is nothing to stop you from cross-examining the witness as to the reasons why he has sought the distortion of his face, and you are entitled to address the Tribunal subsequently on the basis that we should not accept his evidence because he was not brave enough to face up to publicity. That's a matter which is always relevant on the question of protective measures. Anything else you've put forward, I'm afraid the question of principle that has arisen is only that the application was made out of time, and that's not a very -- that's not one which is favourably received by this Tribunal. Is there anything more you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. You may have those protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And as another preliminary matter, you should have before you a copy of a letter the Prosecution has given to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Bring the witness in while we're waiting, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The purpose of this letter is twofold. One is that one of the potential exhibits in this case in the binders was given the number 332. It is, in fact, a set of documents. They're eight separate handwritten documents with the translations, and during the course of the proceedings either the Prosecution or the Defence may refer to these documents, and so what we've done is subnumbered them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, would you. Would you sit down, please, sir, for a moment whilst we're getting this procedural matter sorted out. You can open the rest of the blinds while we're waiting. I'm sorry, Ms. Kuo. We have these eight subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes. So we've taken the liberty of subnumbering them for the ease of reference during the course of the proceedings and, in addition, the second purpose is that we discovered a translation error in what has been numbered as 332/5A, the list of persons who disappeared, and we have attached the corrected version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, would you please stand up and take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One of the microphones is apparently not turned on. The translators couldn't hear. Sit down, please, sir. I can assure the interpreters that the solemn declaration was made. It can go into the transcript as such. Yes, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to have this witness shown a piece of paper which the Prosecution wishes to enter in evidence as the next numbered exhibit. I'm afraid I've lost track of the numbers. Perhaps the registrar can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be 399.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And we ask that this be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac? Any objection to the tendering of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The exhibit will --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The exhibit will be P399, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, on this piece of paper do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Directly above your name are the words "Witness" and then the letters "FWS" followed by the number "215"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You should know, Witness, that because of the protective measures you've requested and the Court has granted, you will be referred to during the course of the trial as Witness FWS-215; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Under your name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I should also let you know that on this piece of paper are also two other names, and following those names are also numbers. If you wish to mention those names at all in your testimony, please use the numbers instead of the names; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir, what ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In 1992, in April, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Which part of Foca specifically did you live in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: The centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that a predominantly Serb or Muslim area, or was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: According to the latest census, the centre of the town was predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you married, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In April 1992, how old were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: My son was born in 1971, and my daughter, in 1973.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Before the war started in Foca, what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On what day did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Before the 8th of April, 1992, had people in your neighbourhood begun to take protective measures in anticipation of some sort of conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: There were some signs, some indications, and as a citizen, I heard that there were some guards on duty in some parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was there a joint guard organised in your building before the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Prior to the 8th of April, there were no organised guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: At some point were organised guards formed, after the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On what date; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, it was, at any rate, before the 8th, when the fighting began, so between the 8th and the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the day that the war in Foca started. Did you go to work that day, the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes, I was on my way to work, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992, how many people came to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Only I and Okica Simovic came.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of your colleague who came to work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why the other people weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen at some point that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, I can say that as I was going to work I noticed something curious in front of the building of the court, which is right next to my building. And then as I walked next to the municipal hall and the police building - this is the morning rush-hour - so I saw there were some people. I saw some commotion, some melee of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: (redacted), did something happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At that moment, nothing, nothing yet. So I entered the building, as always, because I had the key to the front door. We unlocked the door, entered the building, and I didn't observe anything out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: At some time that morning did shooting start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes. It happened at sometime around half past nine in the morning. A powerful infantry -- I'm not a military man, but I think it was infantry fire that was opened all over the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, because in that part of the town, in front of the square, one could only see people fleeing in panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: With this colleague of mine with whom I had come to work, we decided it wasn't really wise to be there all on our own, so we decided to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did you go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: So near the fire brigade centre is the post office, and behind that, our residential buildings. So we entered one of those buildings, the entrance, and we found there 15 or 20 frightened people, and that included some uniformed policemen, who, I suppose, at that time were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What were they doing there, the policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, they simply thought that they found a shelter on the staircase, in that entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you stay in that building with those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: For a very short while because we wanted to get back home as quickly as possible. So we decided to try to run across and through some side streets so as to get back home as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: We did that, perhaps, after about 10 or 15 minutes, because it is not that far away. But we were indeed frightened because there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you got home, was your family at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At that moment only my children were there. My wife had also gone to work together with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did your wife return at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: She returned about an hour after I did because she worked a bit further away, a bit further away from the place where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the shooting continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: The shooting was still on. And she arrived home in a car; a colleague of hers from work had driven her home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where did you and your family stay from that point on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: We mostly stayed at home in the building where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you hide in a specific part of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Together we tried to organise a hideaway in the basements of the apartment buildings where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were there times when you went upstairs to your apartment building -- to your apartment? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the residents of your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At that moment when I returned, my family and I were the only Muslims there. All the rest of our neighbours were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On those occasions when you went upstairs to your apartment, were you able to see outside what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Of course. We used every convenient moment to peek behind the curtains and to see whether there was anyone there and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you saw from your windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, nothing but people running across the street. People were running in fright from one place to another. These were probably friends, relatives, who tried to stay together as close as possible, believing that they would be safer that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see houses burning at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, certainly in that period, from all sides one could see that houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you at that time recognise any of the owners of those houses who owned the houses that were burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I must admit that I personally did not know all the people from that part of town. No, no, I could not mention the names of the owners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many days did you and your family hide like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, actually, this lasted all the way up to the 23rd of April, 1992, when I was taken away from home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Prior to the 23rd of April, was there a time when the fighting within Foca ceased, stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: The fighting stopped intermittently. And whenever there wasn't any strong shooting or strong explosions, we tried to get out of buildings, in front of buildings, so that we could simply comment upon these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was there a time when a longer ceasefire was called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: There were periods when this lasted shorter and when it lasted longer. Actually, one could say that during the day the ceasefire would go on for longer, and during the night the shooting was more intensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did something happen on the 14th or 15th of April, 1992 in terms of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: On the 14th and 15th, as far as the fighting is concerned, I have nothing special to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know when Foca fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, I think it was that period precisely. Everything happened very fast, seven or eight days, from the 8th to the 14th or 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And on the 14th or 15th of April, who took over Foca town? What entity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot state with certainty whether all of Foca was taken or occupied at that time, but certain parts certainly were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were there public announcements made to the people in terms of what they should do at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, when there was electricity, we could listen to Radio Foca, and the calls were made to citizens to go out to carry out their work duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know who controlled Radio Foca at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Like some other citizens, I took advantage of the moments when the shooting would abate to go out to town for awhile. Perhaps this was too brave and naive. I actually went to the centre of town, to the army building where Radio Foca was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you learn when you went there? Who was in charge or had taken over Radio Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At that moment there were quite a few persons in uniform in front of this particular building. From contacts with some other citizens, we found out that these were some persons who came from elsewhere. Actually, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you hear comments on Radio Foca with regard to the relationship between Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At one moment as I listened to Radio Foca, I could hear the then Minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Velibor Ostojic, who spoke for about 50 minutes. This was a speech based on propaganda, stating that there could be no life for the Serbs and Muslims together, that it was impossible to live together anymore, that there would be no more friendships, no more kum relations, no more good neighbourly relations. This remained imprinted in my mind, and that speech was quite alarming - very alarming - for any honest person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What other public institutions in Foca became Serb controlled at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I could say that this was the building of the court of the Municipal of the Assembly, the building of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs and the building of the fire brigade (redacted), of course, including the radio station or the building of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, you mention that had there were calls to people to go back to work. Did you try to go back to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I tried on two or three occasions to go to my building because I felt that the institution where I worked was the humane one. Since there were lots of fires in town, I felt that I should be there at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened the first time you tried to go to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: The first time, I found some people there. The building had already been broken into from the entrance side. The glass had been broken and the door was broken down. One of the previous employees was there, together with two or three other men. Together we went to the upper floor of this building, and we noted that the part of the building that had been rented out to a certain person had been partly looted and had been broken into.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was the person that that place was rented out to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Nebojsa Krnojelac was the name of this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And did you observe any other damage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Certainly. I went to my office and I immediately noticed that the entrance door had been broken into by shots fired from firearms and the lock was blown out. Then also there were many holes in the ceiling. The ceiling was riddled. Also where Tito's picture was, there had been a lot of shooting there, and a lot of the things were just thrown about the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you stay at work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No. I just looked at my desk. It was locked properly. There was nothing missing from the desk at that point in time. Having realised what the situation was, I withdrew or, rather, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you go back a second time to your office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes. The second time I tried, after a day or two, to go there. A man stopped me at the very entrance. He was a Serb, an ethnic Serb. He told me that I was not allowed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you explain who you were and what your purpose was in going there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: That man knew me well. I tried to talk to him as we walked, and we walked all the way up to the building, and I said to him, "Well, you know that I worked here for many years, and I want to get in," and he said, "No."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that man dressed in civilian clothes or a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Civilian clothes. But the other person who was inside -- there were two or three men who I knew very well. One of them was certainly wearing a military uniform. In front of the building, there was also a military vehicle, a so-called Pitzgaur.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you given any explanation for why you could not go inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: One of them was called Milic Milos, and I tried to ask whether I could do anything, whether I could help. He drove me away very rudely. He said, "Get lost. Otherwise, I'm going to call the military police to take you to prison."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the individuals who were dressed in uniform, were they Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: At that moment, all who were there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did your wife try to report to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes. She tried to report to work. She was persistent. She went back, she phoned, but she was always told to wait some more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you or your wife ever go back to work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: My wife did not indeed, but I was naive, and I tried to go there one more time. I passed by the building, and I went up towards the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened that third time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: In the part called Sahat Kula, a man ran up to me. He was wearing a military uniform and he had a rifle. He stopped me and he told me that I had to go back with him. I returned to the square, frightened, where this superior of his was waiting for me. He wore a camouflage uniform. He had a beard, and also a machine-gun at his chest. I'm sorry. I have to say that my wife was with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did that man say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: That man said, as soon as he saw me, "I have to arrest you."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did he arrest you at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I asked him, "May I know why?" He paused for a few moments and looked at me and said, "All right. Go home now."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you recall what date that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: The 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And were you actually arrested then at a later point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No. I went home, and I spent that day quite restless and frightened. But then on the next day, the 23rd of April, around 9.30 in the morning, in the presence of my son and daughter and in the absence of my wife, who had gone to town to get some supplies, my arrest took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions about your arrest in a moment, but before that, when you were able to walk around Foca, were you able to see the damage that had happened and was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I managed to pass through the old part of town only once when everything had already been burned down and destroyed. I passed in fear, and unconsciously I went down to the marketplace and the army building and then all the way to my home. All of it was really awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say the "old part of town," what is that part called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Stara Carsija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that a predominantly Serb or Muslim part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I think that the buildings where craftsmen worked were mostly Muslims, although there were some shops where Serbs worked as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see people setting fire to houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: In the period when there is shooting, one could see that the houses of certain people were being targeted. In Prijeka Carsija, in Stara Carsija, a person who was craftsman, for a long time we saw that his house was being fired at with inflammable bullets and indeed it did catch fire. Since all of these buildings were leaning one against the other, the other houses were set fire to as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the craftsman whose house you've described as being targeted, was he a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see any attempts to put out fires?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No. At that moment, since I, (redacted), did not have access to these buildings to put the fires out, then indeed nobody else could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see houses in Sukovac burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you see how that came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: One could see that there were some people who were walking around who would approach certain houses and then a fire would appear, and then, of course, the entire building would start burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "certain people," were they wearing anything distinctive or did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: No. It was too far away to be able to recognise a person. But they were carrying something on their backs. Probably this was some kind of inflammable material in order to be able to set the building on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the certain buildings that were set on fire in this way, could you tell whether the residents were Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, in apartment buildings the population was mixed. There were Serbs and Muslims in others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Is Sukovac a mixed neighbourhood or is it predominantly Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: I think that one could say that it was a Muslim neighbourhood to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During this same time, could you see people being arrested, your neighbours, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: In the part of the neighbourhood of Ribarsko one could notice Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that. This was very close to the building where I lived. One could notice persons in uniform moving about, especially in the part where the Ribarsko building is, where there was a large concentration of people who were gathering there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see how people were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was arresting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Persons in uniform, in camouflage uniforms, and there were also civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Are you asking about the ethnicity of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes. Let's start there. What ethnicity were the people who were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Well, they were primarily Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The people being arrested, were they civilians or were they wearing military clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Primarily civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "primarily," do you also mean that there were people in uniform being arrested or do you mean that everybody you saw being arrested was in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: It would be better to put it this way: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they men or women who were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: Men only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell their age -- the range of their ages, who appeared to be the youngest person and who appeared to be the oldest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-215
utterances.text: There were both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I see that we're coming to the end of the day, and I think that we can continue with this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us about these papers that have been handed in relating to Witness 66, the "east side stories"? I think somebody has described it as a diary. Is this going to go into evidence, or is it just like one of the statements that we refer to only if it is referred to in the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Witness 66 is being handled by my colleague, Bill Smith, and I believe that these are documents that were prepared by the witness himself. I'm not entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because for my own part, I never read any of the OTP statements because they're not in evidence; and if they do go into evidence, then I will read them. Now, I don't want to read this in advance if it's not going to go into evidence. It's not like the transcript, for example, from the Kunarac trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I think it's meant more as analogous to the statements that we've been giving for people to prepare if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of November, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
